title: Writing Intensive Aspects
text:
Question 1 - How do writing assignments and writing instruction further the learning objectives of this course and how is writing integrated into the course? Note that the syllabus must reflect the critical role that writing plays in the course.
Understanding the organization of a complex software system, how potentially adversarial inputs and actors can affect the system, and methods to mitigate these threats requires strong written communication to be effective – if team members cannot convey why a threat should be considered, or why it works, or how to address a threat, resources may not be devoted to fix security problems. Developing skills to communicate about software and threats is thus equally important to developing skills to find and address these threats. Writing is integrated into the course through the regular submission of long-form reports as well as short-form exercise responses.
Question 2 - What types of writing (e.g., research papers, problem sets, presentations, technical documents, lab reports, essays, journaling etc.) will be assigned? Explain how these assignments meet the requirement that writing be a significant part of the course work, including details about multi-authored assignments, if any. Include the required length for each writing assignment and demonstrate how the minimum word count (or its equivalent) for finished writing will be met.
The primary writing assessment will be in the form of 4 lab reports detailing four separate software systems the students examine for potential vulnerabilities, the process by which they are examined, and the vulnerabilities and mitigation strategies that result. Each report should be 4-5 pages and involve figures that communicate the details of the system and vulnerabilities in sufficient detail to be replicated by others. The typical audience of such a report would be other software professionals and technical managers.
Since the final reports may be produced collaboratively, each student in a group will be required to submit a draft of at least 1 of the 3 required sections (roughly 1200 words) and provide a written critique (150 words each) of each section drafted by other group members, so that each lab report will require 1400-1500 words of writing.
In addition, students will also complete bi-weekly problem sets involving shorter descriptions of threats and mitigations. These problem sets will typically involve 400-500 words of writing and grading will have a writing quality component.
Question 3 - How will students’ final course grade depend on their writing performance? What percentage of the course grade will depend on the quality and level of the student’s writing compared to the percentage of the grade that depends on the course content? Note that this information must also be on the syllabus.
Lab reports will account for 45% of the final grade, and bi-weekly problem sets will account for 15% of the final grade. Thus 60% of the course grade will be based on writing-focused assignments.
Question 4 - Indicate which assignment(s) students will be required to revise and resubmit after feedback from the instructor. Indicate who will be providing the feedback. Include an example of the assignment instructions you are likely to use for this assignment or assignments.
Students are expected to apply draft feedback from their group members in producing each lab report, and instructor feedback on lab reports to future reports. Instructors will provide feedback on lab report writing quality, and all lab report instructions will include instructions reminding students to review the feedback on previous reports and submit a short explanation of how feedback was incorporated. Written exercise solutions – graded by teaching assistants ­– that receive a low writing quality score can be revised and re-submitted for writing quality.
Question 5 - What types of writing instruction will be experienced by students? How much class time will be devoted to explicit writing instruction and at what points in the semester? What types of writing support and resources will be provided to students?
Throughout the semester examples of presenting the architecture of various types of software systems (applications, operating systems, network protocols) will be given in class, with an early emphasis on architectural diagrams, which are an important part of the computer science WEC plan that are not covered in many other classes. Example threat models and vulnerability reports will be used in the explanation of these concepts, and presented along with opportunities to critically analyze the presentation before each lab report is due.
Question 6 - If teaching assistants will participate in writing assessment and writing instruction, explain how will they be trained (e.g. in how to review, grade and respond to student writing) and how will they be supervised. If the course is taught in multiple sections with multiple faculty (e.g. a capstone directed studies course), explain how every faculty mentor will ensure that their students will receive a writing intensive experience.
Teaching assistants will be trained in writing assessment by grading a small subset of submissions for each exercise set along with the instructor, in addition to reviewing rubrics for the writing quality grades (based on the criteria set forth in the department WEC plan) for each of these exercise sets before they are due.

Computing technology has profound effects on society and is strongly affected by society. This provides many benefits and also presents many challenges. title: Syllabus
text:
Use of AI tools
Since written communication is a learning outcome of this course, the content of your individually authored papers and journal entries must be your own writing. AI tools may be used for grammar and clarity editing of your own prose, but not to generate the substance of the writing that forms the basis of the Writing Intensive assessment. All AI assistance must be acknowledged and cited.
AI tools should also NOT be used to summarize readings. You should train your brain to read and reflect on what you are reading, and make connections. We will be using a social reading tool where you can interact with your classmates, so that hopefully the reading will be more meaningful.
In this class, the ability to write is essential for understanding and communicating your perspectives on social, legal and ethical issues in computing. As such using Generative AI tools for summarizing the readings and generating any part of your written assignments is NOT permitted.
GenAI tools are not substitutes for your intellectual effort or scholarly expression. Active engagement with course materials, critical thinking and judgment, and expression of original ideas should never be outsourced to technology.
Any violation of this is subject to the UMN’s Scholastic Dishonesty policy included in the Board of Regents: Student Conduct Code. This includes incorporating any part of an AI-generated text in an assignment.
Violations will be subject to a zero grade on the assignment in question and a letter grade reduction in the final grade. In addition, the incident will be reported to the Office for Community Standards.
The Board of Regents Student Conduct Code states the following in Section IV, Subd.1: Scholastic Dishonesty:
“Scholastic dishonesty means plagiarism; cheating on assignments or examinations, including the unauthorized use of online learning support and testing platforms; engaging in unauthorized collaboration on academic work, including the posting of student-generated coursework on online learning support and testing platforms not approved for the specific course in question; taking, acquiring, or using course materials without faculty permission, including the posting of faculty-provided course materials on online learning and testing platforms; …”
If you are in doubt as to whether you are using an online learning support platform appropriately in this course, I encourage you to discuss your situation with me.
Any assignment content composed by any resource other than you, regardless of whether that resource is human or digital, must be attributed to the source through proper citation.
Unattributed use of online learning support platforms and unauthorized sharing of instructional property are forms of scholastic dishonesty and will be treated as such.
I do provide guidance to you in your assignment descriptions on when the use of AI is appropriate (and permitted). In these LIMITED instances, when using AI tools, you are going to be asked to:

Include proper citation for any AI-generated text, images, or other media. An example citation might look like this:

Copilot, Microsoft Copilot, accessed [Month] [Day], [Year], cloud.copilot.microsoft.com

Include an AI disclosure statement. For example:

“For this assignment, I used [list of AI tools used in assignment] for [specific purpose, e.g., generating an outline, summarizing sources, grammar revision] but not for [list of student contribution, e.g., direct content creation.]”


You may be asked to show proper documentation of your process as required by the assignment. Students are responsible for any data input into AI tools and the AI-generated outputs they choose to include in their coursework.
Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted information into AI systems, including personal information, research data, or any instructional or peer-generated materials from this course. The Student Conduct Code and University copyright policies prohibit students from uploading or sharing instructor or peer course materials (e.g., lecture notes, assessments, readings, discussion posts) with AI tools or external platforms. I will never upload your work to any GenAI tools for teaching or research purposes. Tools may generate false, misleading, biased outputs and illicitly reproduce copyrighted materials. You are responsible for vetting all generated responses before using them in your work. Any violation of this course policy, including failure to disclose or adequately cite AI use when required may be considered Scholastic Dishonesty in accordance with the Student Conduct Code and the Office for Community Standards Consequences & Outcomes. Violations will be subject to a final grade penalty, and failing the assignment. In addition, the incident will be reported to the Office for Community Standards. As the AI landscape evolves globally and at the UMN, this policy is subject to revision at any point throughout the semester. Students will be alerted to any changes via a Canvas announcement.

Instrumentalism

Technology is a neutral tool – it is neither good nor bad
Technology does not contain inherent moral values
Humans have complete control over how it is used
High human agency – society decides whether technology is used for good or bad


“Guns don’t kill people, people kill people.”

Technology shapes human behavior and society

title: Rules of Engagement
text:
It is expected that everyone will participate in a mature and respectful fashion.
Participate actively in the discussions, having completed the pre-review material and thought about the issues.
Throw sunlight, not shade. Like beautiful flowers, we are here to learn and grow together. This will involve discussing difficult topics and challenging some of our deepest held beliefs and assumptions with curiosity and respect. In order to do that, your actions and behavior should support the growth and learning of others. You should find ways to acknowledge disagreement while also supporting the growth and dignity of your colleagues. This means that hostile reactions such as eye-rolls, yelling, teasing, or otherwise throwing shade will not be accepted.
Disagree with ideas, but do not make personal attacks. Do not demean or embarrass others. Do not make sexist, racist, xenophobic, homophobic, transphobic, or victim-blaming comments. Immature, aggressive, or disrespectful behavior (i.e., the various ways we can throw shade and hate on one another) will not be tolerated.
Be cautious of how you use humor. Tone is often difficult to gauge when you don’t know people very well (not as well as you do at a friendship level). Some common forms of humor such as sarcasm can be interpreted as hurtful and demeaning by others. Be aware of the potential impact of your words, regardless of the intentions. Think through your comments before you say them.
Be open to be challenged or confronted on your pre-conceived ideas. The academic classroom is a place where we learn to examine social issues through scientific inquiry. It is no place for uninformed biases.
Communicate in “I” statements. Don’t tell others what to do or think as if it is a command. Instead, describe your own perspective or experience. Speak for yourself; don’t volunteer other people to speak. Consider when it is appropriate to speak from your own experience and when it is better to consider the text or listen to others.
Study and avoid engaging in rhetorical fallacies.
Avoid making broad generalizations you can’t back up with evidence (e.g.,“everyone everywhere always does x”). Acknowledge when your personal experience is too limited or privileged to be generalized.

title: Role of Writing
text:
This is a Writing Intensive course, and written communication is a core learning outcome.
Writing in CSCI 4970W mirrors the documentation practices of professional software engineering and research: writing is carried out iteratively, collaboratively where appropriate, and always with the goal of producing documentation that is complete, clear, and technically rigorous. Writing in this course takes several forms:
GitHub Documentation Milestones. The core writing in this course is the staged GitHub documentation of your project across three milestones: (1) design documentation, (2) implementation documentation, and (3) testing documentation. Each milestone is submitted as a pull request, reviewed by the instructor for completeness, clarity, and technical rigor, and then revised and merged. This staged, feedback-and-revision structure is the heart of Writing Intensive pedagogy in this course: you are expected to take instructor feedback seriously and to produce substantially improved revised documentation in response to it.
Individually Authored Pull Requests. For team projects, each student is expected to lead a distinct portion of the documentation for each milestone and to submit that portion as their own pull request. This allows writing to be assessed individually even when the underlying project work is collaborative. Revisions to the initial submissions may be made by the full team, but all teammates are expected to contribute approximately equally across the three milestones.
Lab Notebooks. Each student maintains an individual lab notebook throughout the semester, beginning in Week 1. The lab notebook is an ongoing written record of your technical work: what you tried, what you learned, what decisions you made, and why. Lab notebooks are reviewed during the Implementation Clinic phase and contribute to individual written communication assessment. Lab notebooks must be the student’s own work.
Architecture Presentation. A 20-minute oral presentation delivered to the instructor in Week 7 serves as a companion communication assessment. You will identify the specific technical challenge your project addresses and present your proposed system architecture, connecting your design to prior work and existing systems.
Use of AI tools. Because this is a project course, you are allowed and encouraged to use AI tools, forums, code repositories, and other external resources to help solve technical problems, as long as you appropriately credit those sources. However, because written communication is a learning outcome of this course, the content of your individually authored documentation pull requests and lab notebook entries must be your own writing. AI tools may be used for grammar and clarity editing of your own prose, but not to generate the substance of the writing that forms the basis of the Writing Intensive assessment. All AI assistance must be acknowledged and cited.

title: Technology Analysis
text:
What makes a good choice
A good choice is a technology where thoughtful people genuinely disagree. If you can write the “against” section in two minutes and the “for” section is a strawman, pick something else. Look for a technology where:

There is a real, identifiable benefit that someone would miss if it disappeared.
There is a real, identifiable harm that falls on someone.
The benefit and the harm often land on different people.
The dilemma survives good intentions — it is not simply a case of a company behaving badly, but a case where even a careful, well-meaning designer faces a hard tradeoff.

Examples of the shape of a workable dilemma (do not feel limited to these): proctoring software that detects cheating and also flags disabled students; a predictive model that allocates scarce medical care; content moderation at a scale that requires automation; a dating app’s matching algorithm; smoking- or driving-behavior logging that lowers insurance premiums for some and raises them for others.

The Patents List page, or a patent you find yourself through Patent Public Search. Patents are useful because they state, in the applicants’ own words, what the technology is for — which is often revealing.
Reporting from an outlet with an accountable editorial process. A vendor’s own marketing page or blog post is a primary source about the vendor’s claims, not a description of the technology; you may cite it as evidence of what the company says, but it cannot be your only source.

You do not need to get your article approved, but if you are unsure whether your choice presents a real dilemma, ask me or a TA before the first draft. Discovering at the final-draft stage that your technology has no genuine second side is an expensive problem to fix.

title: Technology Analysis
text:
What “independent” arguments means
Two arguments are independent if knocking one down leaves the other standing. “This tool saves teachers time” and “this tool lets teachers spend more hours with students” are the same argument wearing two hats. “This tool saves teachers time” and “this tool gives students feedback at 11pm when no teacher is available” are independent — they would appeal to different people and rest on different evidence.
Write the arguments you disagree with at their strongest. Steelman, don’t strawman. A reader should not be able to tell from your “against” section which way you are going to land.

title: Technology Analysis
text:
What “who decides” means
Don’t rush this part, it carries real weight in the rubric. It is not enough to say “the government should regulate it” or “stakeholders should be consulted.” Be specific about which actors, on what question, and why that actor rather than another. Candidates include: the engineers who build it, the company that owns it, the people it is used on, the people it is used by, professional bodies (recall the ACM Code of Ethics, regulators at the city, state, or federal level, courts, unions, affected communities who were never consulted. Different actors have specific standing over different decisions. For example, who deploys the technology might be a different question from who governs the data it collects.

Moral disagreement becomes impossible
Many philosophers – especially those involved in computing and ethics – find subjectivism and relativism problematic. For example, if each person or culture can decide what is morally acceptable, how can we ever agree at all on norms, policies, and appropriate behavior?

title: Ethics Frameworks
text:
Moral disagreement becomes impossible

If I say “abortion is wrong” (= I disapprove) and you say “abortion is permissible” (= I don’t disapprove), we’ve both spoken truly and we aren’t actually contradicting each other. We’re doing the equivalent of me saying “I like cilantro” and you saying “I don’t.” That’s not a disagreementm it’s a pair of biographical reports.

section: Not a matter of taste or opinion
text:
Not a matter of taste or opinion

If the culture’s code defines what is right, then abolitionists in 1830s America, suffragists, and dissidents in any repressive regime were wrong at the time
Cultures aren’t discrete. Who counts as “the culture”? A country, a religion, a generation, a subreddit? Everyone belongs to many overlapping groups with conflicting norms.

There are values that hold regardless of individual beliefs

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
What happened

1996 flight of the European Space Agency’s (ESA) new Ariane 5 rocket
About 37 seconds after lift-off, the rocket veered off course, began to break apart, and self-destructed
Payload: the four Cluster satellites, a scientific mission to study Earth’s magnetosphere
Cost: roughly US$370 million in rocket and payload (commonly cited figure), on top of a decade of development
No one was killed

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
section: Why study a failure where no one died?
text:
Why study a failure where no one died?

It is one of the most expensive software bugs in history
The bug itself was small and well understood
The failure was not really about one line of code; it was about assumptions, reuse, testing, and organizational decisions
It raises a question we will keep returning to: who is responsible when a complex system fails?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The technical cause (in plain terms)

The rocket’s Inertial Reference System (SRI) tells the flight computer where the rocket is and how it’s moving
Code from a previous successful Ariane version was reused
One calculation converted a 64-bit floating-point number (related to horizontal velocity) into a 16-bit signed integer
Ariane 5 was faster than Ariane 4
The value was too big to fit which caused an operand error (overflow) with the exception not handled

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The cascade

The backup SRI hit the error and shut down (it ran the same software)
72 milliseconds later, the primary SRI hit the same error and shut down
The primary SRI sent a diagnostic bit pattern to the flight computer
The flight computer read the diagnostic data as if it were flight data
It commanded full nozzle deflection → extreme angle of attack → aerodynamic forces tore the rocket apart → self-destruct

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The twist
The calculation that failed served no purpose after lift-off.

It was part of an alignment function only needed before launch
On Ariane 4, it kept running for ~40 seconds after lift-off, a feature that allowed a quick restart if the countdown was held
Ariane 5 did not need this feature, but it was kept because “it worked” and changing it was seen as a risk

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Why wasn’t it caught?
From the Inquiry Board report (Lions et al., 1996):

The specifications did not include Ariane 5 trajectory data
No full system test was run

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Key quote

“The exception which occurred was not due to random failure but a design error. The exception was detected, but inappropriately handled because the view had been taken that software should be considered correct until it is shown to be at fault. […] The Board is in favour of the opposite view, that software should be assumed to be faulty until applying the currently accepted best practice methods can demonstrate that it is correct.”
– Ariane 501 Inquiry Board Report, 1996

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Aftermath

The Inquiry Board issued 14 recommendations (e.g., turn off functions not needed in flight, test with real equipment, have sensors send best-effort data instead of stopping)
The Cluster mission was rebuilt (Cluster II) and launched in 2000 on Russian Soyuz rockets
Ariane 5 went on to become one of the most reliable launchers, including launching the James Webb Space Telescope (2021)
Scientists lost years of work
European taxpayers paid for the loss

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Who dunnit?
Computer scientists disagreed about what the “real” lesson was:

Programming view (Jézéquel & Meyer, 1997): it was a reuse error; explicit preconditions (design by contract) would have documented the assumption and caught it
Systems engineering view (Nuseibeh, 1997): the problem was requirements and specification; no single person or practice is to blame
The Inquiry Board pointed to the whole development and testing process

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The problem of many hands
Helen Nissenbaum (1996), written the same year as Flight 501, identifies barriers to accountability in computing:

the problem of many hands: so many people contribute that no one feels responsible
the problem of bugs: treating software errors as inevitable, “just how software is”
blaming the computer: “the computer did it”
software ownership without liability: vendors disclaim responsibility

Which of these do you see in Ariane 5?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Connection to professional codes
ACM Code of Ethics:

2.1 Strive to achieve high quality in both the processes and products of professional work
2.5 Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of computer systems and their impacts, including analysis of possible risks
2.6 Perform work only in areas of competence

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Group Discussion 1: Responsibility

Who is responsible for the failure of Flight 501? List every person or group you can think of (the original Ariane 4 programmers, the Ariane 5 team, managers, testers, ESA, the contractors…).
Is it fair to blame the programmers who wrote correct code for Ariane 4?
Does “no single person is to blame” mean “no one is responsible”?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Group Discussion 2: Reuse and assumptions

The code was reused because it was proven reliable. When does reuse make systems safer, and when does it make them more dangerous?
The overflow protection was removed for performance reasons. How should engineers weigh efficiency against safety margins?
Today we routinely use open-source libraries, APIs, pre-trained models built for other contexts, and LLM-generated code. What are the risks in modern software?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Group Discussion 3: Testing and culture

“It worked on Ariane 4” was treated as evidence of correctness. What is the difference between a system that has not failed and a system that is correct?
The full system was never tested with real equipment, partly because of cost. Who should decide how much testing is “enough,” and on what basis?
Would you speak up if you noticed an untested assumption close to a launch deadline? What would make it easier or harder?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Group Discussion 4: Ethics frameworks
Each group takes one framework:

Consequentialism: Who bore the costs of the failure? Would the outcome judgment change if the payoff had been astronauts instead of satellites?
Deontology: What duties did engineers and managers have, regardless of the outcome? Which ACM principles were violated, if any?
Virtue ethics: Which of Vallor’s technomoral virtues (e.g., humility, perspective, technomoral wisdom) were missing?
Contractualism: Could the decision to skip full system testing be justified to everyone affected?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
Bringing it forward
Ariane 5 is not an isolated case. Compare:

Patriot missile, Dhahran (1991): a floating-point rounding error accumulated over time; 28 soldiers killed
Therac-25 (1985–87): reused software from an earlier machine, with the hardware safety interlocks removed
Boeing 737 MAX (2018–19): software designed around assumptions about a single sensor and about pilot response

What patterns do you see across these cases?

title: History of transformative technologies: Automation bias
text:
Three recurring patterns
When we look back at the history of transformative technologies, some patterns keep repeating:

Automation bias: trusting software more than people, including ourselves
Unequal harms: the costs fall mostly on marginalized groups
Reactive regulation: regulation/laws arrive only after a disaster

We will look at each pattern through historical cases and timelines.

title: History of transformative technologies: Automation bias
text:
What is automation bias?
Two kinds of errors (Skitka, Mosier, & Burdick, 1999):

Omission: failing to act because the system didn’t flag a problem (missed events when not explicitly prompted about them by the aid)
Commission: following the system’s recommendation even when other evidence contradicts it (did what an automated aid recommended, even when it contradicted their training and other 100% valid and available indicators)

title: History of transformative technologies: Automation bias
text:
Why does it happen?

Software seems objective and neutral
Checking the system takes time and effort
Trusting the system becomes the default
When the system says the person is wrong, the person has to prove the system is wrong

Year
Event

Case: UK Post Office Horizon scandal
Accounting software showed cash shortfalls at local post offices. The Post Office blamed the sub-postmasters who ran them.







Year
Event

Fujitsu’s Horizon system rolled out; courts in England and Wales now presume computers work correctly unless shown otherwise

title: History of transformative technologies

Case: Robodebt (Australia, 2016–2019)
An automated system that calculated welfare “overpayments” and sent debt notices.



Year
Event




2016
System launched: it averaged annual tax income across fortnights, which assumed steady income


2016–2019
About 470,000 debts wrongly issued; recipients had to prove they did not owe the money

Group Discussion: Automation bias

Was the continued use of the accounting system despite reports of balancing errors an failure of omission or commission?

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
Who bears the risk?

Technologies are often tested on and deployed first on people with the least power to refuse (welfare recipients, immigrants, prisoners, poor neighborhoods)
When the system fails, those groups have the fewest resources to fight back
Their complaints are often less likely to be believed


Automated systems “manage the poor so that we do not have to” – Virginia Eubanks, Automating Inequality (2018)

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
A historical parallel: Bhopal (1984)

A gas leak at a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, killed thousands of people and injured hundreds of thousands

The same pattern shows up in physical and digital technologies.

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
Tombstone regulation

In aviation safety, “tombstone mentality” means waiting for deaths before fixing a known problem
Laws and regulators usually react to disasters rather than prevent them
Recall Moor’s policy vacuum and regulatory lag from last week

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
The Collingridge dilemma
David Collingridge, The Social Control of Technology (1980):

Early on, a technology is easy to change, but we don’t know its harms yet
Later, the harms are clear, but the technology is entrenched and hard to change


By the time we know enough to regulate, it may be too late to regulate easily.

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
Is proactive regulation possible?
Some counterexamples:

1975, Asilomar: scientists paused and set guidelines for recombinant DNA research before any harm
1987, Montreal Protocol: countries phased out CFCs soon after the ozone hole was discovered, before the worst damage
2024, EU AI Act: bans some AI uses (e.g., social scoring) and sets rules by risk level before most harms occur
2025, Australia: minimum age of 16 for social media accounts

Critics argue proactive regulation can slow innovation or target the wrong risks. Supporters point to the precautionary principle (Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 15).

title: History of transformative technologies
text:
Group Discussion: Reactive regulation

Why do laws usually come after disasters? Think about who has information, money, and power before and after.
In most of our cases, someone warned about the problem before the disaster. Why weren’t they heard?
Is the EU AI Act a solution to the Collingridge dilemma, or does it just move the problem?
If you could pass one proactive law about AI today, what would it be? What disaster would it be trying to prevent?

Unequal harms: the targets were people on welfare, many of them in financial crisis
Reactive regulation: action came only after court cases, a class action, and a Royal Commission

1996 flight of the European Space Agency’s (ESA) new Ariane 5 rocket

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
section: Why study a failure where no one died?
text:
Why study a failure where no one died?

It is one of the most expensive software bugs in history
The bug itself was small and well understood
The failure was not really about one line of code; it was about assumptions, reuse, testing, and organizational decisions
It raises a question we will keep returning to: who is responsible when a complex system fails?

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The technical cause

The rocket’s Inertial Reference System (SRI) tells the flight computer where the rocket is and how it’s moving
Code from a previous successful Ariane version was reused
One calculation converted a 64-bit floating-point number (related to horizontal velocity) into a 16-bit signed integer
Ariane 5 was faster than Ariane 4
The value was too big to fit which caused an operand error (overflow) with the exception not handled

title: Case Study: Ariane Flight V88
text:
The technical cause
The calculation that failed served no purpose after lift-off.

It was part of an alignment function only needed before launch
On Ariane 4, it kept running for ~40 seconds after lift-off, a feature that allowed a quick restart if the countdown was held
Ariane 5 did not need this feature, but it was kept because “it worked” and changing it was seen as a risk

title: Algorithmic Bias
text:
Case: Amazon’s hiring tool (2014–2017)

Amazon built a machine learning tool to rate job applicants’ résumés
Trained on 10 years of résumés submitted to the company
The model learned to penalize résumés containing the word “women’s” (e.g., “women’s chess club captain”) and downgraded graduates of two all-women’s colleges
Engineers removed those terms, but could not guarantee the model would not find other proxies

“the tool disadvantaged candidates who went to certain women’s colleges presumably not attended by many existing Amazon engineers”

title: Algorithmic Bias
text:
Case: Health care algorithm (2019)
Obermeyer et al. (2019), Science studied a widely used algorithm that decides which patients get extra care:

The algorithm predicted health care costs as a proxy for health care needs
Less money is spent on Black patients who have the same level of need (unequal access to care)
Result: Black patients assigned the same level of risk are sicker than White patients
This racial bias reduces the number of Black patients identified for extra care by more than half

Race was not an input. The bias came from using health care costs.

title: Algorithmic Bias
section: Proxies: “Fairness through unawareness” does not work
text:
Proxies: “Fairness through unawareness” does not work
Removing a protected attribute (race, gender) from the data does not remove bias, because other features act as proxies:

Zip code → race (a legacy of redlining)
Name, college, hobbies, language choice → gender
Cost of care → race
Gaps in employment → disability, caregiving, gender

The model learns patterns in the data, and the data carries history.

Can you identify any bias in those decisions? What proxies do you think are used in college admissions decisions?
How can engineers build models that take into account preexisting bias (historical roots), technical bias (design and architecture limits), and emergent bias (feedback loops, changing environments, and user adaptation)?

title: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness
text:
Many definitions of fairness

individual fairness: the goal of giving similar individuals similar decisions
group fairness: the goal of giving similar decisions across demographic groups

Discrimination manifests itself in unequal treatment of groups.

title: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness
text:
The impossibility result
Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017) showed:
When base rates differ between groups, a (non-perfect) classifier cannot satisfy calibration/predictive parity and equal false positive and false negative rates at the same time.

Fairness is not a bug to be fixed with better code
Choosing a fairness definition is a value choice, not a technical one
Someone must decide which errors matter most, and for whom

title: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness
text:
Fairness and the law
US anti-discrimination law (e.g., Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act) recognizes:

Disparate treatment: intentionally treating people differently because of a protected characteristic
Disparate impact: a neutral-looking practice that disproportionately harms a protected group (Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 1971)
The EEOC’s four-fifths rule: a selection rate for one group below 80% of the rate for the highest group is evidence of adverse impact

Most algorithmic bias looks like disparate impact, not intent.

title: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness
text:
Fairness in generative AI

Image generators asked for “a CEO” or “a doctor” produce mostly white men; “a fast-food worker” produces mostly people with darker skin (Bloomberg analysis of Stable Diffusion, 2023)
Attempts to correct this can overcorrect: in 2024, Google paused Gemini’s image generation of people after it produced historically inaccurate images (e.g., racially diverse 1940s German soldiers)
Language models can associate names, dialects (e.g., African American English), and identities with negative traits

What would “fair” output even look like for a generative model?

title: Disinformation
text:
Information disorder
Wardle & Derakhshan (2017) distinguish three types:

Misinformation: false information shared without intent to harm (e.g., sharing a fake cure you believe works)
Disinformation: false information shared knowingly to deceive or harm (e.g., state-run influence campaigns)
Malinformation: true information shared to cause harm (e.g., leaking private information, doxxing)

Intent matters for ethics, but the harm can be the same.

title: Disinformation
text:
Disinformation is not new

Propaganda, forged documents, and rumors are as old as politics
What computing changed:

Scale: anyone can reach millions
Speed: content spreads faster than it can be checked
Cost: creating convincing fake content is now nearly free
Targeting: messages can be tailored to specific audiences
Amplification: algorithms decide what we see

title: Disinformation
text:
Falsehood spreads faster
Vosoughi, Roy & Aral (2018), Science studied ~126,000 stories on Twitter (2006–2017):

False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news
True stories took about 6 times longer to reach 1,500 people
False news was more novel and evoked surprise and disgust
Bots spread true and false news at similar rates, so humans, not bots, drove the difference

title: Disinformation
text:
Engagement-based ranking

Social media feeds are ranked to maximize engagement (clicks, likes, comments, shares, time on site)
Content that provokes outrage and surprise gets more engagement
2018: Facebook shifted its News Feed to prioritize “meaningful social interactions”
Internal documents leaked by whistleblower Frances Haugen (2021) showed Facebook had weighted the “angry” emoji reaction five times more than a “like” (Washington Post, 2021)
Engineers optimized a metric; the metric shaped what billions of people saw

title: Disinformation
text:
Do algorithms cause polarization?
The evidence is more mixed than headlines suggest:

2023 studies with Meta during the 2020 US election (Guess et al., Science) switched users from algorithmic to chronological feeds
Users spent less time on the platform and saw more untrustworthy content, but there were no significant changes in polarization over three months
Algorithms are one factor among many (cable news, political elites, offline networks)

Why might it be hard to study the effects of platforms on society?

title: Disinformation
text:
Synthetic media

Deepfakes: AI-generated audio, image, or video that depicts people saying or doing things they never did
2023: Days before Slovakia’s parliamentary election, a fake audio clip of a candidate discussing how to rig the vote spread online
2024: Voters in New Hampshire received robocalls with an AI-generated voice of President Biden telling them not to vote in the primary

The FCC ruled AI-generated voices in robocalls illegal under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and fined the political consultant behind the calls $6 million

Non-consensual intimate deepfakes overwhelmingly target women and girls

title: Disinformation
text:
The liar’s dividend
Chesney & Citron (2019):

As people learn that audio and video can be faked, it becomes easier for liars to dismiss real evidence as fake.


The harm of deepfakes is not only that people believe false things
It is also that people stop believing true things
Who benefits most from a world where nothing can be verified?

Content moderation is weaker in non-English languages. Recall Facebook in Myanmar
Disinformation campaigns often target marginalized communities (e.g., voter suppression messages aimed at specific groups)
Those with less access to reliable information or media literacy resources have fewer defenses

Step 1: Define the problem and the app
Pick a real-world issue (e.g., food insecurity on campus, finding accessible housing, coordinating care for an aging parent, reporting unsafe working conditions) and sketch an app that addresses it. One paragraph is enough at this stage: who is the app for, and what problem does it solve? Pick an issue where the people most affected have something real at stake. title: Paper 2 - Application
section: Step 2: Prepare and conduct the interview
text:
Step 2: Prepare and conduct the interview

Who to interview. Interview at least one person who could realistically use the app. They should be an adult (18+). The best interviewee is someone with direct experience of the problem, not just a friend who is willing to talk to you.
Write your questions in advance. Prepare 8–12 open-ended questions covering:

their experience with the problem and how they deal with it now
what they would want the app to do (use cases and desired functionality)
what would make them not use it, or worry about using it
what data they would and would not be comfortable sharing, and with whom
who else (family members, employers, landlords, etc.) could be affected by the app

Ask follow-up questions. The most useful material usually comes from “Can you tell me more about that?” Don’t just read the list.
Get consent and protect your interviewee. Before you start, tell them what the interview is for, that it is for a class assignment, and that they can skip any question or stop at any time. Ask before recording or taking notes. Use a pseudonym in your paper and leave out identifying details. Do not ask them to disclose information they would be harmed by if it became public. Include a copy of your questions in an appendix at the end of your paper.
Interviews should be about 20–30 minutes. Take notes during the interview, and write up any other ideas you had during the interview right after while they are fresh.

Then compare the two sets of answers. Useful questions to ask yourself:

What did the human raise that the LLM didn’t (and vice versa)?
Which answers were more specific? More surprising? More generic?
Did the LLM reflect any assumptions or stereotypes about the kind of person it was asked to be?

Step 2: Design and run your tests

Use paired (counterfactual) inputs: identical inputs that differ only in the attribute you are testing. For example, the same resume with only the name changed.

The impossibility result
Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017) showed:
When base rates differ between groups, a (non-perfect) classifier cannot satisfy calibration/predictive parity and equal false positive and false negative rates at the same time.

Choosing a fairness definition is a value choice, not a technical one
Someone must decide which errors matter most, and for whom

title: Fairness
text:
Fairness and the law
US anti-discrimination law (e.g., Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act) recognizes:

Disparate treatment: intentionally treating people differently because of a protected characteristic
Disparate impact: a neutral-looking practice that disproportionately harms a protected group (Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 1971)
The EEOC’s four-fifths rule: a selection rate for one group below 80% of the rate for the highest group is evidence of adverse impact

Most algorithmic bias looks like disparate impact, not intent.
Laws generally only apply in employment, credit, and housing

title: Fairness
text:

Image generators asked for “a CEO” or “a doctor” produce mostly white men; “a fast-food worker” produces mostly people with darker skin (Bloomberg analysis of Stable Diffusion, 2023)
Attempts to correct this can overcorrect: in 2024, Google paused Gemini’s image generation of people after it produced historically inaccurate images (e.g., racially diverse 1940s German soldiers)
Language models can associate names, dialects (e.g., African American English), and identities with negative traits

What would “fair” output even look like for a generative model?

title: Disinformation
text:
Information disorder
Wardle & Derakhshan (2017) distinguish three types:

Misinformation: false information shared without intent to harm (e.g., sharing a fake cure you believe works)
Disinformation: false information shared knowingly to deceive or harm (e.g., state-run influence campaigns)
Malinformation: true information shared to cause harm (e.g., leaking private information, doxxing)

Intent matters for ethics, but the harm can be the same.

title: Disinformation
text:
Disinformation is not new

Propaganda, forged documents, and rumors are as old as politics
What computing changed:

Scale: anyone can reach millions
Speed: content spreads faster than it can be checked
Cost: creating convincing fake content is now nearly free
Targeting: messages can be tailored to specific audiences
Amplification: algorithms decide what we see

title: Disinformation
text:
Falsehood spreads faster
Vosoughi, Roy & Aral (2018), Science studied ~126,000 stories on Twitter (2006–2017):

False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news
True stories took about 6 times longer to reach 1,500 people
False news was more novel and evoked surprise and disgust
Bots spread true and false news at similar rates, so humans, not bots, drove the difference

title: Disinformation
text:
Engagement-based ranking

Social media feeds are ranked to maximize engagement (clicks, likes, comments, shares, time on site)
Content that provokes outrage and surprise gets more engagement
2018: Facebook shifted its News Feed to prioritize “meaningful social interactions”
Internal documents leaked by whistleblower Frances Haugen (2021) showed Facebook had weighted the “angry” emoji reaction five times more than a “like” (Washington Post, 2021)
Engineers optimized a metric; the metric shaped what billions of people saw

title: Disinformation
text:
Do algorithms cause polarization?
The evidence is more mixed than headlines suggest:

2023 studies with Meta during the 2020 US election (Guess et al., Science) switched users from algorithmic to chronological feeds
Users spent less time on the platform and saw more untrustworthy content, but there were no significant changes in polarization over three months
Algorithms are one factor among many (cable news, political elites, offline networks)

Why might it be hard to study the effects of platforms on society?

title: Disinformation
text:
Synthetic media

Deepfakes: AI-generated audio, image, or video that depicts people saying or doing things they never did
2023: Days before Slovakia’s parliamentary election, a fake audio clip of a candidate discussing how to rig the vote spread online
2024: Voters in New Hampshire received robocalls with an AI-generated voice of President Biden telling them not to vote in the primary

The FCC ruled AI-generated voices in robocalls illegal under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and fined the political consultant behind the calls $6 million

Non-consensual intimate deepfakes overwhelmingly target women and girls

title: Disinformation
text:
The liar’s dividend
Chesney & Citron (2019):

As people learn that audio and video can be faked, it becomes easier for liars to dismiss real evidence as fake.


The harm of deepfakes is not only that people believe false things
It is also that people stop believing true things
Who benefits most from a world where nothing can be verified?

title: Disinformation
text:
Unequal harms, again

Content moderation is weaker in non-English languages. Recall Facebook in Myanmar
Disinformation campaigns often target marginalized communities (e.g., voter suppression messages aimed at specific groups)
Those with less access to reliable information or media literacy resources have fewer defenses

First Amendment: limits government restrictions on speech, not private companies’ moderation decisions

title: Quiz: Sources of Bias Across the ML Life Cycle
text:
Quiz: Sources of Bias Across the ML Life Cycle
Suresh & Guttag (2021). For each scenario, pick the source of bias that best describes what went wrong.
Choices (same for every question):

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias


Question 1
An image search engine returns mostly photos of men when users search for “CEO.” The engineers check the results and find that they match the real gender breakdown of Fortune 500 CEOs. Even so, the results reinforce the stereotype that leaders are men.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: a. Historical bias Feedback: The data accurately reflects the world, but the world itself reflects past and present inequality. Even perfect sampling would not fix this.

Question 2
A startup builds a skin cancer detection app. Almost all the training images come from a dermatology clinic whose patients are mostly light-skinned. The app works well for light skin but often misses melanoma on darker skin.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: b. Representation bias Feedback: People with darker skin are under-sampled in the training data, so the model does not learn their patterns well.

Question 3
A company wants to identify its most “productive” remote employees. Since productivity is hard to observe directly, the model uses the number of hours each employee shows as “active” in the chat app. Employees who do focused work offline, or who use assistive technologies that interact differently with the app, get rated as less productive.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: c. Measurement bias Feedback: “Active hours in the chat app” is a poor proxy for productivity, the thing the company actually cares about.

Question 4
A hospital builds one model to predict diabetes complications for all patients. Research shows that a key blood marker in the model relates to diabetes risk differently across ethnic groups. Because the model uses a single relationship for everyone, it makes worse predictions for some groups, even groups that are well represented in the data.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: d. Aggregation bias Feedback: A single model is applied to groups whose features relate to the outcome in different ways.

Question 5
To run a speech recognition model on cheap phones, engineers compress it by removing the parts of the network that contribute least to overall accuracy. Overall accuracy barely changes, but accuracy for speakers with less common accents drops sharply.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: e. Learning bias Feedback: A modeling choice (compression that optimizes for overall accuracy) made the performance gap between groups larger.

Question 6
A company advertises that its face detection system is “99% accurate.” That number comes from a popular benchmark dataset in which most faces are lighter-skinned men. When the system is sold to customers around the world, it fails much more often on darker-skinned women.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: f. Evaluation bias Feedback: The benchmark used to measure performance does not represent the people who will actually use the system, so the reported accuracy is misleading.

Question 7
A school district builds a model to flag students who might benefit from extra tutoring. A few years later, the district starts using the same scores to decide which students are allowed into advanced placement courses.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: g. Deployment bias Feedback: The system is being used for a purpose it was not designed for, turning a support tool into a gatekeeping tool.

Question 8
A bank trains a loan approval model on 30 years of its own lending records. The records are complete and accurate. However, for decades the bank (like many others) denied loans in neighborhoods that had been redlined, so applicants from those neighborhoods have fewer successful repayment histories. The model learns to give lower scores to applicants from those areas.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: a. Historical bias Feedback: The data is accurate but reflects decades of discriminatory lending. The injustice is in the world the data records.

Question 9
A wearable fitness tracker estimates heart rate using a light sensor on the wrist. The sensor gives less accurate readings on darker skin. A health insurance company uses the tracker’s heart rate data as a feature to predict health risk.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: c. Measurement bias Feedback: The feature is measured with different accuracy for different groups, so the data is noisier for some people than for others.

Question 10
A sentiment analysis model is trained on a large collection of social media posts from all users. Certain slang terms and emoji mean something positive in one online community but something negative in the general population. The single model reads these posts the same way for everyone and misclassifies posts from that community.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: d. Aggregation bias Feedback: One model is used for groups where the same features (words, emoji) have different meanings.

Question 11
A voice assistant is trained on recordings collected by asking volunteers to call a phone line. Most volunteers were college students in the U.S. The assistant struggles to understand older adults and people who speak English as a second language.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: b. Representation bias Feedback: The way the training data was collected left out large parts of the population that will use the system.

Question 12
A team training a medical model adds “differential privacy” noise during training to protect patients’ data. Model accuracy drops only a little for the majority group, but drops a lot for patients from small minority groups, because the model now has a harder time learning from their few examples.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: e. Learning bias Feedback: A training choice (adding privacy noise) widened the performance gap between groups.

Question 13
A tool designed to give radiologists a “second opinion” on X-rays is adopted by an understaffed rural clinic. With no radiologist on staff, the clinic’s nurses treat the tool’s output as the final diagnosis.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: g. Deployment bias Feedback: A system meant to support expert judgment is being used in place of it, in a context the designers did not intend.

Question 14
Researchers compare chatbots using a well-known test set of questions. The test set was written entirely in standard American English by graduate students. The top-ranked chatbot is chosen for a public health hotline serving many immigrant communities, where it performs much worse than its ranking suggested.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: f. Evaluation bias Feedback: The benchmark used to rank the models does not represent the population the system will serve.

Question 15
A hospital system wants to identify patients who need extra care. Since “health need” is hard to measure directly, the model is trained to predict how much money each patient will spend on health care next year. Patients who face barriers to getting care, such as cost, distance, or distrust of doctors, spend less even when they are just as sick, so the model ranks them as lower need.

Historical bias
Representation bias
Measurement bias
Aggregation bias
Learning bias
Evaluation bias
Deployment bias

Correct answer: c. Measurement bias Feedback: The label (health care spending) is a poor proxy for the thing the hospital actually cares about (health need), and the gap between the two is larger for some groups than for others.

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Case: Gender Shades (2018)
Buolamwini & Gebru (2018) audited commercial gender classification systems (IBM, Microsoft, Face++):

Built a new benchmark balanced by gender and skin type (existing benchmarks were mostly lighter-skinned men)
Error rates of up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women vs. at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men
Intersectional analysis: looking only at gender or only at skin type hides the worst disparities

Which source of bias does this reveal?

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Case: Actionable Auditing (2019)
Raji & Buolamwini (2019) asked: did the audit change anything?

The audited companies were notified and released new versions of their products
All three audited companies reduced their error disparities
Companies that were not audited (e.g., Amazon, Kairos) had large disparities in the new tests

Public, named audits can create accountability. But companies also pushed back on the findings, and audits put researchers at legal and reputational risk.

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Case: Facebook ad delivery (2019)
Ali et al. (2019) ran ads with identical targeting (same audience, same budget):

Ads for jobs in the lumber industry were delivered to audiences that were mostly white men
Ads for janitor jobs were delivered mostly to Black women
Housing ads were skewed by race depending on the image in the ad
The skew came from Facebook’s optimization for engagement, not from the advertiser’s choices

In 2022, the U.S. Department of Justice settled with Meta under the Fair Housing Act. Meta built a “Variance Reduction System” for housing ads.

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Legal risks of auditing

Scraping audits and sock puppet audits often violate a website’s terms of service
Researchers feared prosecution under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Sandvig v. Barr (2020): a federal court ruled that violating terms of service for research does not, by itself, violate the CFAA
Van Buren v. United States (2021): the Supreme Court narrowed the CFAA’s scope
Platforms have still shut down researchers’ accounts and tools (e.g., Meta and NYU’s Ad Observatory, 2021)

Who benefits when audits are hard to do?

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
NYC Local Law 144 (2023)
New York City requires employers that use automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) to:

Have an independent bias audit done each year
Publish a summary of the audit results
Notify candidates that an AEDT is being used

The audit must report selection rates and impact ratios by sex, race/ethnicity, and intersectional categories.
\[\text{impact ratio} = \frac{\text{selection rate of a category}}{\text{selection rate of the most selected category}}\]
Recall the EEOC’s four-fifths rule: an impact ratio below 0.8 is evidence of adverse impact.

0.30/0.30 = 1.00


Women
60/300 = 0.20
0.20/0.30 = 0.67


Nonbinary
5/20 = 0.25

Women fall below the four-fifths threshold
The nonbinary category has very few applicants: is a ratio based on 20 people reliable? (NYC rules allow excluding categories under 2% of the data)
Notice what this audit does not measure: whether the people advanced were qualified (true/false positive rates)

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Limits of Local Law 144
A study of the law’s first year (Wright et al., 2024) found:

Very few employers published audits (18 of 391 employers studied)
Employers decide for themselves whether their tool counts as an AEDT
The law only requires reporting: there is no penalty for a low impact ratio
Audits measure selection rates only, not accuracy, validity, or disability discrimination

Is an audit that no one is required to act on still useful?

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Internal audits
Raji et al. (2020) proposed an end-to-end internal audit framework (SMACTR) that runs through the development life cycle:

Scoping: what are the intended uses and the possible harms?
Mapping: who are the stakeholders and who is responsible?
Artifact collection: documentation such as model cards and datasheets for datasets
Testing: e.g., disaggregated evaluation and adversarial testing
Reflection: weigh results against the company’s ethical principles, and decide whether to go ahead

Open-source tools can help: Fairlearn, IBM AI Fairness 360, Aequitas

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Who audits the auditors?
Costanza-Chock, Raji & Buolamwini (2022) surveyed people working in the audit field and found:

There are no shared standards for what an audit must include
Second-party auditors are paid by the company being audited (conflict of interest)
Results are often kept private
Affected communities are rarely involved

Audit-washing: using a (weak) audit to make a system look fair without changing it

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Group Activity: Present Technology
AI hiring tools: many companies use automated tools to screen résumés, rank candidates, analyze video interviews, or score games and assessments (e.g., HireVue, Workday, LinkedIn Recruiter).
In 2023, a lawsuit (Mobley v. Workday) claimed Workday’s screening tools discriminated by race, age, and disability. In 2025 a court allowed the age discrimination claim to move forward as a collective action.
Your group is hired to design an audit of an AI hiring tool:

What type of audit (first-, second-, or third-party) and which method would you use? What access do you need?
Which groups and which intersectional categories would you test? Which fairness metrics would you report?
What would count as “failing” the audit, and what should happen if the tool fails?
What harms might your audit miss?

title: Disinformation

Warm-up
Before we start, answer in your journal:
Think of the last time you shared (or almost shared) something online that turned out to be false or misleading.

Why did it seem believable?
How did you find out it was false?

title: Disinformation
text:
Information disorder
Wardle & Derakhshan (2017) distinguish three types:

Misinformation: false information shared without intent to harm (e.g., sharing a fake cure you believe works)
Disinformation: false information shared knowingly to deceive or harm (e.g., state-run influence campaigns)
Malinformation: true information shared to cause harm (e.g., leaking private information, doxxing)

Intent matters for ethics, but the harm can be the same.

title: Disinformation
text:
Disinformation is not new

Propaganda, forged documents, and rumors are as old as politics
What computing changed:

Scale: anyone can reach millions
Speed: content spreads faster than it can be checked
Cost: creating convincing fake content is now nearly free
Targeting: messages can be tailored to specific audiences
Amplification: algorithms decide what we see

title: Disinformation
text:
Falsehood spreads faster
Vosoughi, Roy & Aral (2018), Science studied ~126,000 stories on Twitter (2006–2017):

False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news
True stories took about 6 times longer to reach 1,500 people
False news was more novel and evoked surprise and disgust
Bots spread true and false news at similar rates, so humans, not bots, drove the difference

title: Disinformation
text:
Engagement-based ranking

Social media feeds are ranked to maximize engagement (clicks, likes, comments, shares, time on site)
Content that provokes outrage and surprise gets more engagement
2018: Facebook shifted its News Feed to prioritize “meaningful social interactions”
Internal documents leaked by whistleblower Frances Haugen (2021) showed Facebook had weighted the “angry” emoji reaction five times more than a “like” (Washington Post, 2021)
Engineers optimized a metric; the metric shaped what billions of people saw

title: Disinformation
text:
Do algorithms cause polarization?
The evidence is more mixed than headlines suggest:

2023 studies with Meta during the 2020 US election (Guess et al., Science) switched users from algorithmic to chronological feeds
Users spent less time on the platform and saw more untrustworthy content, but there were no significant changes in polarization over three months
Algorithms are one factor among many (cable news, political elites, offline networks)

Why might it be hard to study the effects of platforms on society?

title: Disinformation
text:
Synthetic media

Deepfakes: AI-generated audio, image, or video that depicts people saying or doing things they never did
2023: Days before Slovakia’s parliamentary election, a fake audio clip of a candidate discussing how to rig the vote spread online
2024: Voters in New Hampshire received robocalls with an AI-generated voice of President Biden telling them not to vote in the primary

The FCC ruled AI-generated voices in robocalls illegal under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and fined the political consultant behind the calls $6 million

Non-consensual intimate deepfakes overwhelmingly target women and girls

title: Disinformation
text:
The liar’s dividend
Chesney & Citron (2019):

As people learn that audio and video can be faked, it becomes easier for liars to dismiss real evidence as fake.


The harm of deepfakes is not only that people believe false things
It is also that people stop believing true things
Who benefits most from a world where nothing can be verified?

title: Disinformation
text:
Unequal harms, again

Content moderation is weaker in non-English languages. Recall Facebook in Myanmar
Disinformation campaigns often target marginalized communities (e.g., voter suppression messages aimed at specific groups)
Those with less access to reliable information or media literacy resources have fewer defenses

title: Disinformation
text:
What can be done?



Approach
Example
Trade-off




Content moderation
Removing posts, banning accounts
Who decides what is false? Censorship concerns


Fact-checking and labels
Third-party fact-checkers; X/Meta Community Notes
Slow; may not reach those who saw the original


Changing ranking
Downranking borderline content
Platforms lose engagement (and revenue)


Provenance
Watermarks, C2PA content credentials
Can be stripped; does not cover all content


Prebunking / inoculation
Teaching manipulation techniques in advance (Roozenbeek et al., 2022)
Effects may fade over time


Regulation
EU Digital Services Act (2022) requires large platforms to assess systemic risks
Different values about speech across countries



2025: Meta ended its third-party fact-checking program in the US and moved to Community Notes.

title: Disinformation
text:
Platforms and the law (US)

First Amendment: limits government restrictions on speech, not private companies’ moderation decisions
Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996): platforms are generally not liable for content posted by users, and can moderate in good faith
Section 230 was written for the internet of 1996. Does it still fit platforms that actively rank and recommend content?

Recall the policy vacuum and the Collingridge dilemma from the reactive regulation lecture.

title: Disinformation
text:
Group Discussion: Ethics frameworks

Consequentialism: Is it better to remove some true content by mistake, or leave some false content up? Who bears the costs of each error?
Deontology: Do platforms have a duty to tell the truth, or only a duty not to lie? Do users have a duty to verify before sharing?
Contractualism: Could an engagement-maximizing ranking algorithm be justified to everyone affected, including those harmed by what it amplifies?
Political economy: Who profits from engagement? Who pays for disinformation?

title: Disinformation
text:
Group Discussion: Disinformation

You are an engineer asked to improve “engagement” by 5%. What questions would you ask before starting?
Who should decide what counts as disinformation: platforms, governments, users, independent fact-checkers?
Should AI companies be responsible for deepfakes made with their tools?
How is disinformation connected to algorithmic bias? (Think about what gets amplified and whose content gets moderated)

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Who does the audit?

The results of first-party audits are not typically disclosed to the public and there is little transparency about whether their recommendations are implemented.
While second-party auditors are an important part of the ecosystem, there is no standardized audit methods and disclosure policies
Third-party audits are conducted by fully independent organizations or individuals with no obligation or contractual relationship to the audit target
Third-party audit have been particularly influential in creating public awareness of algorithmic harms

Costanza-Chock, Raji & Buolamwini (2022)

title: Algorithmic Audits
text:
Audit methods

Audit study: systematically probing and testing of black-box systems through repeated interaction to understand their behavior and investigate deficiency (discrimination, bias, or something else) without direct access to the internals of the system
Purposefully intended to be external evaluations
Audit studies are a powerful tool for establishing evidence of discrimination, especially disparate impact
